en/obras/guia-1.md:2.translation:
Well, I'm starting to write this series of Howtos, which, although
they don't reveal great knowledge, clearly outline some basic points
that are very useful when getting into a system as multifaceted as
this one. I think I'm going to leave a copy of each one on my blog in case
someone wants to take a tour through them.

en/obras/guia-1.md:8.translation:
You've surely
come across comments in forums or people who directly tell you:
"the correct name is GNU/Linux, if you say just Linux then
you're only referring to the kernel."

en/obras/guia-1.md:10.translation:
To me personally, it
seems a bit ridiculous to be so demanding about names, but
these attitudes have their reasons that go back to the principles
of our beloved penguin.

en/obras/guia-1.md:14.translation:
It
is said that in the beginning there was man, and for a while he was
good. Then man created computers in the image and likeness of his
television. jejeje.

en/obras/guia-1.md:16.translation:
What is counted, however, is that at the
beginning of the computer age, the real business was not the software,
but the computer itself. The software was written by any user
with moderate knowledge, and computing professionals freely shared
their creations, which quickly spread around the world and
achieved that phenomenal technological development that has characterized
computing.

en/obras/guia-1.md:18.translation:
But then companies started to realize that
software was something from which they could gain profit, and they
began to create restrictive rules so that their employees would
not disclose their developments and so that the companies could sell them.

en/obras/guia-1.md:20.translation:
These
attitudes were spreading throughout all the companies and the
information stopped flowing. A systems expert named Richard Stallman,
who was used to sharing and receiving information freely,
was working in a company that had just purchased a new printer.

en/obras/guia-1.md:22.translation:
That
printer wasn't working as the company needed, and, as a
good expert, Ricardito saw that the problem was in the printer's
controller.

en/obras/guia-1.md:24.translation:
So, just as he had done on other occasions,
he picked up the phone and asked how much they would
charge him for providing the source code of the driver, since he
wanted to make a correction, which he would later send to the manufacturer
to consider adding to their future versions. But his surprise
was huge when they told him they couldn't deliver the source code,
not even for sale.

en/obras/guia-1.md:26.translation:
After causing a telephonic revolt, gathering
great courage, and ending up with not a single line of code, Stallman
realized that around him companies were already protecting their source
code and simply thought: "This is no longer good."

en/obras/guia-1.md:28.translation:
By discussing
with other experts, they decided to bring an end to all of
this, so they created the FSF (Free Software Foundation), the
GPL licenses, and began working on a new operating system
filled with completely free applications and drivers. This system would
be named GNU (GNU is Not Unix).

en/obras/guia-1.md:30.translation:
It was the year of 1992 and
the system was already very complete, with hundreds of applications, but the
most important thing was missing, the core.

en/obras/guia-1.md:32.translation:
Although the system
wasn't completely finished, many wanted to use it already, but
without that core it was impossible to do so. Then came a
blessing in the form of a core from Linus Torvalds, who had
developed a core which he called Linux, which had been conceived
initially to be used in Minix systems.

en/obras/guia-1.md:34.translation:
However, it wasn't
very difficult to integrate it into the GNU system, and, many years before
it was expected, the first usable version of GNU, called GNU/Linux, emerged.

en/obras/guia-1.md:36.translation:
It
should be noted that GNU/Linux is not the pinnacle of success, since
GNU and Linux are independent projects that support each other
only. The main goal of the FSF is to have its own kernel, of which
we already have prototypes under the name of Hurd.

en/obras/guia-1.md:40.translation:
I will
conclude by mentioning that at some point the native core of GNU will be
completed and promises major improvements over the current Linux kernel, which,
since its creation, has also never stopped improving.

en/obras/guia-1.md:42.translation:
However,
enjoy GNU/Linux for now knowing that thousands of people
are working to improve it. Although the system
currently does impressive things, when the GNU kernel is
finished, you'll see what a truly robust, stable,
intelligent, and capable system is.

en/obras/paquetes-y-dependencias-en-gnu-.translation:
One of the main problems with GNU/Linux since its inception
has always been standardization. And it's that GNU/Linux has
always been an open project for everyone, where thousands of hands
have created a small piece of code. But, after all, humans are
not always going to agree, and with so many hands involved, it's
difficult to have order, since each person can have a Linux completely
different from what their neighbor has.

Then application
developers have a big problem: When they create their
program, they use different libraries to save work and
check that it works correctly on their system. But if the developer
wants to distribute it, it's very likely that
other computers don't have the same libraries that they used or
simply that they are in a different directory than expected,
which makes their program incompatible with other systems.

This
creates a major problem that was initially attempted to be
solved through LSB (Linux Standard Base), which proposed
a set of standard libraries that programmers could rely
on to always find in any Linux system.

However, this plan
did not progress as expected, and LSB became a solution that was not
well accepted, as there were serious discussions about which library
was better than another, a program that caused instability with
another, or that was too unsafe, and it ended with the breaking of relations
with some important companies.

And until a few years
ago, installing a program on Linux was a nightmare, because
to have it you had to find and install every single program
required to make that program work.

A first
solution was the installation packages. A user who wanted to install
a program had to look for the respective installation package (.deb,
.ebuild, .rpm, etc.) for their system, and the installer system
checked the program's dependencies, warning if any were missing and
sometimes suggesting where to download the missing program.

Later, some
of these installation systems could download the installation
packages for the missing programs (dependencies) to make
the user's life much easier.

Users
who migrate from one system to another are surprised to find that
they no longer have to spend hours searching the internet for
a program to install, but instead find a list of programs to install
within their Linux system.

A repository is that, a list of
programs that is maintained by the large number of users
and developers of a particular distribution. Every time a new program
or a new version of it appears, a group of enthusiasts reviews
the dependencies of that program, installs them, and checks
their stability, security, and various conflicts with other
applications. After a period of testing, the program is placed
in the list of "stable programs" where regular users can use it
with full confidence.

Recognize
the installer system being used; for Red Hat and Fedora, YUM is used,
for those coming from Debian, APT is used, for Gentoo it's PORTAGE,
and sorry if by ignorance I omitted any.

- look for the latest stable version of the program
- calculate the number of dependencies for the
program - download all the necessary files to install the program and its dependencies -
verify that the downloaded files are not corrupted (either due to an error in the download or because someone very bad - has altered the package) -
decompress all the files - install
all the programs - configure
all the programs - display options
for things that require the user's attention (such as accepting contracts or providing specific equipment details). And with
that, your program will be installed...

If
the command line isn't your thing, almost all distributions now
come with a graphical interface for their installer. That executes
those three simple commands for you, so all you have to do
is: find the program, select the one you want to install, and
click "Install"...

Every
repository system is by default set up to use stable
versions of the system, but if you're brave enough, you can
always configure it to use unstable repositories to always
get the latest programs straight from the forge (sourceforge),
and if you find any errors, don't forget to report
them so that, in the next update, it is fixed not only for you,
but for everyone who uses that program.
Good luck, if there are any questions then it's time.

en/obras/usuarios-y-permisos-en-gnu-linu.translation:
Linux
is a pretty secure system because most things are done in
user mode, so what we do in this mode will never damage
the system (unless we have done very stupid things before,
such as changing permissions on important files and
directories).

When in a manual or instruction we indicate that
a command should be used in user mode, we use the character "\$" at the
beginning of the line, for example:

For
the safety of their equipment, when they go to run a command as
administrator, start the session, execute what they need to execute,
and return immediately to user mode, this will save them from making an
error that could be fatal to the system.

**Switching between user mode and Administrator:**

The
most common option to run a command is to open a virtual console (some
program within the graphical environment that shows us the command line in
the purest MS-DOS style). and execute commands. When opening it, we will
see something like:

Some
systems, for security reasons, do not allow you to use the "su" command (Ubuntu
and all its derivatives), but instead come with another quite useful and secure
command: "sudo" (stand in for superuser). This command will allow you to
execute commands as if you were the administrator, but without fully opening the
session, so that you do not need to use the "exit" command.
